For "complete cover" I'm deciding if a covered wound should be classified as closure. I think completely covering a wound with a dressing or graft isn't necessarily the same as closure, so I'm leaning toward not assigning it an is_a relationship to closure.

Moving to "complete debridement," I keep that as a debridement process. The next entry has the same label but was wrongly tagged as a temporal instant, so I'm correcting that to the proper debridement process class.

Then "complete decellularization" fits as a material processing step for removing cells from tissue to make a scaffold, so that stands. And "complete defect closure" clearly belongs under wound closure process since it's about closing a surgical defect.

Moving to DFU healing, I don't think secondary intention applies universally since defects can also be closed surgically or grafted, and wound healing itself isn't among the offered classes, so I'm leaving this one unclassified. "Complete elimination of infection" fits as a disorder elimination process assuming infection counts as a disorder. For "complete epithelial closure," I'm questioning whether it fits as a threshold crossing event tied to a measurement datum — that seems off since it's really just the endpoint of epithelialization, so I'm inclined to leave it unclassified too.

For "complete epithelial coverage quality," I'm treating it as equivalent to being fully epithelialized, so is_a epithelialized seems right. "Complete epithelialization" clearly is_a epithelialization process. For "complete epithelialization healing," I'm weighing whether it should be classified under epithelialization process or wound healing, since it's essentially healing achieved through complete epithelialization — leaning toward keeping it under the epithelialization process classification given the head noun is "healing" but the defining mechanism is epithelialization.

For "complete epithelialisation," I'm keeping it under the same classification as epithelialization. For "complete excision," I'm weighing whether it fits better under OBI's definition of excision as physically removing a substance portion, versus being classified as a surgical treatment process — since in wound care contexts complete excision usually refers to surgical removal of a lesion with clear margins, but the term could apply more broadly, so I'm leaning toward keeping the excision classification.

For "complete expansion," I'm finding this too ambiguous given it could mean tissue expansion, cell expansion, lung expansion, or graft mesh expansion — none of these map cleanly, so I'm leaving it unclassified. For "complete fistula closure," I'm debating whether fistula closure counts as wound treatment, since closure can happen spontaneously through healing rather than surgical intervention, so I'm leaning toward not classifying it as treatment.

For "complete graft take," I'm considering whether this counts as regenerative healing, but since graft take is really about adherence and revascularization rather than tissue regeneration, I'm leaving it unclassified. For "complete granulation quality" and "complete granulation response," I'm keeping these under their existing classifications since granulation tissue formation and degree of granulation fit reasonably well as is.

Moving through the remaining rows — collagen calcium-alginate dressing fits as a type of alginate wound dressing, collagen composition describes the compositional makeup of collagen types in tissue, and collagen content refers to the quantitative amount of collagen present.

Crosslinking is a molecular process forming covalent bonds, not really a form of tissue remodeling, so that one doesn't stand. Similarly, collagen deposition is part of granulation tissue formation during the proliferative phase rather than a distinct kind of remodeling, so that doesn't stand either, though collagen deposition-related protein correctly stands as a protein. I'm now looking at collagen derivatives like gelatin and other breakdown products.

Since a collagen fiber is a bundle of fibrils forming a structural, anatomical entity rather than a simple chemical mixture, it might fit cellular_component territory — GO does have terms like "banded collagen fibril" for extracellular structures, so I'm weighing whether collagen fiber counts as a recognized cellular component.

Going row by row: body habitus fits as morphology, body map system seems like a diagram for marking locations, and I'm weighing whether BMI >30 as an information entity should be classified as a threshold specification.

For BMI >35 as a quality, that's reasonably an increased object quality, so it stands, same for the next row.

Body position is trickier — position/posture isn't quite spatial region, but PATO's "structure" quality (relative position and arrangement of parts) might actually fit posture better than I initially thought.

Since a wrong parent is worse than none, I'll mark body position as none given spatial region doesn't fit.

For body region, gross anatomical part works fine as a broad safe parent — it stands.

Body surface is more ambiguous, since anatomically it's often treated as an immaterial boundary rather than a material structure, so I need to check how FMA and UBERON handle it.

Reconsidering — anatomical entity covers both material and immaterial cases, making it the safest parent for body surface, so I'll change it to that.

Body surface area stays as an area quality, and that classification works even though it's often used as a clinical measure like % TBSA.

For bone, I'm weighing anatomical structure against gross anatomical part, since bone tissue itself isn't a single connected structure when considered as tissue rather than an element.

Bone and soft-tissue reconstruction remains a surgical treatment process, no change needed.

Bone augmentation is tricky — it's a planned surgical procedure for increasing bone volume, not a biological regeneration process, and none of the offered categories fit a procedure like this, so I'm leaving it unclassified.

Bone avulsion raises the question of whether it counts as a wound at all, since an avulsion fracture is fundamentally a fracture injury rather than something involving a skin breach as wound care terminology typically requires.

Weighing the risk of a wrong parent against no parent, I'm inclined to still accept it as a traumatic wound if WONT's wound definition is broad enough to cover tissue disruption generally, and I'll apply this same reasoning consistently to the next row as well.

For bone bridge, I see this as an anatomical structure fitting gross anatomical part, so that stands. But bone bridge formation is trickier — it could be developmental morphogenesis, or it could be part of regeneration during fracture healing, and I'm not sure "formation" in the GO sense cleanly captures a pathological physeal bar forming across a healing fracture.

Moving to bone cement, that's clearly a processed material so it stands. Bone cement filling as a surgical procedure is debatable whether it counts as material processing, but since it transforms inputs into a filled defect, I'll let it stand cautiously. Bone consolidation looks like a phase of fracture healing, essentially union of the bone, which I'm considering as a kind of regeneration process.

For bone curettage, since it's scraping away bone tissue (whether for debridement, biopsy, or tumor removal), the broader "excision" category fits better than "debridement" because removing a portion of substance applies universally here, so I'm switching its classification to excision.

For biofilm-associated infection, I'm considering whether to scope it as wound infection specifically given it's judged in a wound care context, even though biofilm infections also occur on devices. For biofilm-associated persistent infection, I'm thinking through whether disease perpetuation applies, since a persistent infection is itself a disease course phenomenon.

For row 12 specifically, I'm leaning toward none since none of the offered categories like biological_process fit a disease-course phenomenon that isn't a genetically encoded program. Row 13, biofilm-coated bacterium, stands as a kind of Bacteria, and I'm starting to look at row 14 on biofilm disruption.

An infection and an infected wound aren't quite the same thing, though the infection as material disease entity could be read as describing the infected tissue itself — the wound remains the bearer of that infection, so I'm leaning toward accepting this as a material disease entity despite the ambiguity.

Going row by row: a wound-related symptom doesn't necessarily count as a complication process since pain, odor, or exudate aren't inherently complications, so I'd lean toward none there. For the pH change row, a shift in pH isn't the same as an acid or base actively acting on tissue, so that one likely doesn't qualify as an acidity impact process either.

Moving on, a change in wound area isn't the same as a treatment-driven disorder modification process -- wound contraction is one type of area change, not the reverse, so I lean none. Change in wound size similarly isn't necessarily a "wound development process," since shrinkage during healing is only one case. For anatomical structure size regulation, a wound isn't really an anatomical structure, so a change in it doesn't fit regulation either. Change of depth falls under the same treatment-process issue as area and size. For changes in fibril assembly, this seems like a molecular-level process rather than tissue remodeling, since collagen fibril assembly changes don't automatically imply reorganization at the tissue level, though I'm still weighing whether scar-related fibril changes could count.

Looking at shear-stress changes, this is a physical process rather than a biological stress response, and shear stress isn't the same as sustained mechanical pressure, so that doesn't qualify either. For channel patency, I'm thinking about whether "patency" is equivalent to "open" or just a related quality -- it likely means the state of being open, so it probably counts as an open-type quality restricted to channels. The chaperone 14-3-3 entry fits as a protein without issue. Now I'm considering whether a gene counts as a molecule -- since a gene is really a region of DNA rather than a molecule itself, I need to think about how sequence ontology treats genes in this context.

Looking at genes more carefully, since SO treats gene as a kind of biological region which falls under region, that classification should be updated to region rather than molecule. For gene expression as a characteristic, I'm weighing whether this is better understood as a quality, a phenotype, or something else entirely -- expression level could be seen as a quality of a gene product or biological entity.

Moving through the wound-related terms, characteristics of malignant wounds cover odor, exudate, pain, and bleeding rather than just morphology, so I'm leaving that unmapped. Charcoal dressings align well with activated-carbon wound dressings, so that mapping stands.

For the Charcot foot entries, I'm distinguishing between the arthropathy itself (not a diabetic foot ulcer, so unmapped), the active episode (which plausibly involves peripheral neuropathy as a participant in its disease course, so I'll keep that mapping), and the pathogenesis, which is really a disorder development process rather than a disease course, so that needs reconsideration.

I'm also looking at Charcot neuroarthropathy complicated with osteomyelitis — since the head term is Charcot neuroarthropathy with osteomyelitis as a secondary part rather than the core kind, I'm leaving this unmapped by the parthood rule. Similarly, Charcot-related wounds aren't always diabetic foot ulcers since Charcot neuroarthropathy can arise from non-diabetic causes like leprosy or syringomyelia, so I'm not mapping that one either.

Row 18 cell-based skin regeneration stays with tissue regeneration. Row 19 cell-cycle arrest connects to the GO cell cycle terms.

Row 20 cell-cycle regulator is trickier though—it could include proteins like cyclins or p53, but also microRNAs and small-molecule drugs, so no single is_a parent holds for every instance. I'll leave this one unassigned.

Checking the first row, critical colonization fits as a type of bacterial colonization process describing bacteria multiplying without classic infection signs, so that classification holds. Now I'm moving to the second row about gene being a kind of region.

Row 3 on critical extremity ischemia as a form of PAOD checks out since CLI is typically the end-stage manifestation of PAD, even though other causes exist. Row 4's CLTI classification under PAOD also holds given it's defined as PAD with rest pain or tissue loss. For row 5, I'm pausing on whether "critical injury" should really be classified as a Wound, since critical injury in trauma contexts often refers to severity of harm broadly rather than a wound specifically.

Injury is the parent class of Wound, meaning not all injuries qualify as wounds, so I'm leaning toward saying no valid parent exists here rather than forcing an incorrect one. For row 6, I'm questioning whether "critical ischemia" typed as a continuant properly linking to the ischemic quality class makes sense, since clinically it functions more as a disorder like critical limb ischemia under PAOD rather than just a quality descriptor.

I'll leave the typing as continuant and move on. For critically colonized is_a colonized, there's a tension: colonization by definition means bacteria multiplying without invading tissue or eliciting host response, but critical colonization involves bacterial burden causing subtle host response that delays healing — which per IWII 2016 is essentially "covert local infection," putting it awkwardly between colonized and infected.

Given that tension, the safer typing is "degree of microbial burden" rather than forcing it under either colonized or infected, so I'll switch the is_a axiom to that. For the corresponding wound-bearer row, if critically colonized wounds don't cleanly satisfy the colonized definition, then none of the generic offered wound types (colonized, contaminated, infected) quite fit either.

Moving to critically compromised perfusion, this is better captured as a form of ischemia — insufficient blood supply relative to metabolic demand — so I'll reclassify it under ischemic. For Crohn's disease, I'm weighing whether "autoimmune tissue disorder" really applies, since Crohn's is immune-mediated but its autoimmune status remains debated.

Many classification systems like DOID place Crohn's under inflammatory bowel disease/intestinal disease rather than autoimmune, since the aberrant response targets commensal gut flora rather than self-antigens, so I'll go with none. For the Val170Leu substitution, I'm considering whether it should be classified as a pathogenic genetic variant given its disease-specific association.

For the remaining rows, cross-sectional area and "stands" both fit as subtypes of area. A crosslinked gel is a material, but not necessarily a clinical drug product since not all crosslinked gels qualify as wound dressings or drug products, nor purely as polymers since gels include solvent along with the polymer network—so I'm leaning toward none for that one. For crosslinked network as a polymer, I'm weighing whether CHEBI's definition of polymer as a mixture applies here.

Checking crosslinked pectin/starch blend as polymer—since it's a blend of polysaccharides, this counts as a mixture of macromolecules, so it stands. Crude extract as mixture also stands, though it could alternatively be processed material, mixture seems more specific within the chemical branch. For crush as a wound-causing pressure impact process, I'm questioning whether crush necessarily implies wound-causing or sustained force, since it's more broadly a compressive mechanism that can cause injury.

Crush seems better classified as a trauma process rather than requiring sustained pressure impact, since not every crush causes an actual wound. Crush injury as a traumatic wound stands though, since the wound class includes closed wounds that lack an open break in the skin.

For "at risk of infection," I'm weighing whether this applies to the patient generally or specifically to wound infection tendency — in this wound care context it's probably about the wound.
